To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) serotonin, but not catecholamine, system activation was evident in subordinate males following one hour of aggressive interaction; (2) catecholamine systems were activated in subordinate males following prolonged social interaction; (3) adrenergic activation was not evident in noradrenergically dominated brain areas; and (4) epinephrine may play a role in stress accommodation.

(1) serotonin is rapidly (within one hour) activated in subordinate males, (2) adrenergic activation is delayed in subordinate males (one week), and (3) noradrenergics are suppressed in dominant males
the indoleamine system is activated by one hour of social interaction, while the catecholamine systems are activated by one week or more of interaction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neuroendocrine correlates of social status in male lizards.
the effects of social aggression on the central neurochemistry of male lizards, A. carolinensis.
the neurochemical mechanisms of aggression, social status and stress in male lizards.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the central neurochemistry of subordinate male Anolis carolinesis is altered in response to aggression, with changes in indoleamine and adrenergic neurotransmitters, but not noradrenergics, being most prominent and consistent with stress-induced activation of the indoleamine system.
the indoleamine system is activated in the subordinate male following aggressive interaction.
social aggression in male lizards is associated with activation of the serotonergie system and prolonged activation in the adrenergic stress response system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the serotonergic, adrenergic, and noradrenergical systems are all activated by aggression in male A. carolinensis, but that the serotonergics are activated most quickly, the noradrenergics are activated most strongly, and the adrenergics are most persistent.
aggression and social status in male Anolis carolinesis activate the central indoleamine system, and that the adrenergic response to social stress is more complex.
social stress activates the central serotonergic system, and that this activation is greatest in the short term.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social interactions in male Anolis carolinesis are stressful for subordinate individuals.
the central biogenic amine systems of male lizards are activated by aggression.
